title: The ten shabads
hook: ten hymns of longing, including the song from the wilderness

segments.voice: Yesterday, trust in protection: no enemy can harm the one the Lord protects, written by a man who had lost nearly everything. Your line was protected. Where did you say it to yourself? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-five.

Night, in a forest. Tradition places Guru Gobind Singh there after the battle at Chamkaur, alone or nearly so, sleeping on the ground with a stone or a clod of earth for a pillow. A general would plan. A father would weep. Tradition says he sang. And what he sang wasn't a battle song or a lament. It was a love song, addressed to a Friend. It is collected with other hymns of his under one name, and that name is today's word.
screen: `NIGHT, IN A FOREST.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.` → `HE SANG A LOVE SONG.`

segments.voice: Shabad Hazare is the name of a small group of hymns by Guru Gobind Singh, ten of them, set to ragas so they can be sung. They are short, and they share a mood: longing for God, and impatience with anything that pretends to be devotion without the heart in it. One of them, paraphrased, tells the mind how to be a true renunciate: treat your own home as the forest, stay detached inside while you live in the world. No need to run off; take the forest with you. Among the ten is the wilderness song, Mittar pyare nu, haal mureedan da kehna. Tell the beloved Friend how his disciples are faring. Then, paraphrased, the song lists the comforts of home and turns every one of them sour. Without you, a soft quilt is like a sickness. Living in fine houses is like living with snakes. The cup and the flask are like blades. And then the turn: the Friend's bare straw bed is better than a comfortable life in burning mansions. Hear what's happening. The man who has lost everything is not mourning the comforts. He is saying they were never the point. The ground is fine, if the Friend is near. Sikhs sing this song in kirtan, sometimes very slowly. Even without the story, the ache in it carries the meaning. Ten hymns, then, but one thread through all of them: what matters is nearness to the Beloved, wherever you happen to sleep.
screen: `TEN HYMNS, SET TO RAGAS.` · `TAKE THE FOREST WITH YOU.` · `TELL THE BELOVED FRIEND.` · `THE STRAW BED IS BETTER.` · then, large: `TEN HYMNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one. If you can, find a recording of Mittar pyare nu, or any of the Shabad Hazare, and let it play through the sit. You don't need to understand the words. Listen to the shape of the longing in the voice. If you can't play one now, sit with the image instead: the straw bed, the open sky, and a Friend nearby. Notice what you'd keep if the comforts went. If you pray, you can let the name Waheguru ride under the music. The bell holds the time.
Shabad Hazare. Ten hymns of Guru Gobind Singh, set to ragas, full of longing; among them the wilderness song, Mittar pyare nu. Today's word.
Your line: ten hymns. Today, play one of them once more, on a walk or in the car, and let it be the only thing playing. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing the Shabad Hazare of Guru Gobind Singh in kirtan, and Mittar pyare nu is often sung slowly in gurdwaras and at gatherings remembering the Guru's time in the Machhiwara forest.

notes: Mittar pyare nu, haal mureedan da kehna is given in transliteration only; the rest of the song and the Ramkali shabad (re man aiso kar sanniasa) are paraphrased. Please check the paraphrases.
The count of ten comes from the index ('ten hymns'); please confirm that Mittar pyare nu (labeled Khyal) is counted among the ten Shabad Hazare of the Dasam Granth.
The setting in the forest after Chamkaur (Machhiwara in howItsDone), and the stone for a pillow, are told as tradition.
Superlatives about this song (best-known, most sung) were deliberately left out.
No etymology of 'Hazare' is given on purpose. The Gurmukhi spelling ਸ਼ਬਦ ਹਜ਼ਾਰੇ should be checked.
Distinct from Guru Arjan's Shabad Hazare in Raga Majh in the Guru Granth Sahib; not mentioned to avoid confusion, but a Keeper may want a line.
Editor pass: removed 'his sons gone' from the forest scene in the hook and the fork (tradition does not have the Guru knowing all four sons' fate at Machhiwara); softened 'often slowly'.
